devices.name: Equipment Rack
devices.role: The cabinet that holds, cools and organises everything
devices.what: A 19-inch enclosure with 24 rack units (U). One U is 1.75 in (44.45 mm) tall. Every device in the lab is screwed or slid into it.
devices.how: Vertical rails with square holes every U take cage nuts and screws, and the U numbers are printed on the rails. A base with levelling feet carries the weight, and perforated doors let air flow front to back. A power strip (PDU) runs down the rear rail.
uses: Rack & Stack: physical installation is the first milestone
Decabling and tidy-up at the end of the course (Goal 9)
Nightly shutdown ends with a rack review by the instructor

devices.name: KVM Console
devices.role: One keyboard, screen and mouse for the whole rack
devices.what: A 1U pull-out drawer with an LCD screen, keyboard and touchpad that folds into the rack. Behind it is an 8-port KVM switch.
devices.how: KVM stands for keyboard, video, mouse. A thick USB + VGA cable joins a server to one of the 8 rear ports. Choose a port and that server's video appears on the screen, while your keyboard and mouse control it.
uses: Install Proxmox on the hypervisor host (Goal 6)
Stage the Raspberry Pis before they join the air-gapped network (Goal 4)
Nightly shutdown: switch the KVM off, fold it, slide it into the rack
leds: lit: a server is connected / selected

devices.name: Legacy Server
devices.role: Older 1U server kept for practice and comparison
devices.what: A 1U, two-socket Intel Xeon server from Dell's 12th generation. Hot-swap drive bays and an LCD status panel are on the front; two power supplies, iDRAC and gigabit NICs are at the back.
devices.how: Two redundant power supplies share the load, so one can fail without a shutdown. The iDRAC port is a tiny separate computer that lets an admin power the server on or off and see its screen over the network, even when the main system is off.
uses: Legacy host for extra practice VMs
Compare an older server with the R440: bezel, LCD, drive bays
Practise reading server status lights
leds: green: system on · off: system off

devices.name: Hypervisor Host
devices.role: Runs Proxmox VE and the virtual machines
devices.what: A 1U Dell EMC server that runs Proxmox VE, a Type-1 hypervisor. Proxmox is installed on the internal SD module (IDSDM), which leaves the drive bays free for virtual machine data.
devices.how: A Type-1 hypervisor runs straight on the hardware and divides CPU, RAM and storage between virtual machines. The Linux bridge vmbr0 is VLAN-aware, so a VM can be placed on a VLAN with a tag. VM disks live on the NAS and are mounted over NFS.
uses: Hosts the Ubuntu-FTP virtual machine (Goal 6)
Managed from the Proxmox web interface on port 8006
Target of the traffic-analysis and physical-security exercises

devices.name: Core Switch
devices.role: Layer 3 switch: VLANs, routing and DHCP
devices.what: A managed Layer 3 switch with twelve 10-gigabit RJ45 ports (two shared with SFP+ cages), a separate out-of-band management port and a console port at the back.
devices.how: The switch learns which MAC address lives on which port and forwards each frame only there. VLANs split it into separate networks. A trunk port carries several VLANs on one link. A switch virtual interface (SVI) gives each VLAN a gateway address so the switch can route between VLANs.
uses: VLANs, SVIs and inter-VLAN routing (Goal 3)
DHCP server for the data and storage networks
In-band and out-of-band management (Goal 1)
Trunk links to servers and the firewall, access links to hosts
leds: solid: link up · blinking: traffic · off: no link
green: running · blinking: booting · amber: fault

devices.name: Secondary Switch
devices.role: A second identical switch for extra segments and practice
devices.what: The same CBS350-12XT hardware as the core switch. Identical hardware means a config learned on one works on the other.
devices.how: Works exactly like the core switch. Used as spare capacity or as a separate segment, depending on what the instructor assigns.
uses: Extra switching capacity or a second segment
Practise factory reset and sanitising (Goals 1 and 9)
Compare running-config and startup-config on two units
leds: solid: link up · blinking: traffic · off: no link

devices.name: Firewall
devices.role: Perimeter firewall between the lab and the (simulated) Internet
devices.what: A compact next-generation firewall that sits between the lab LAN and the WAN. In this lab the WAN side is a simulated ISP, so nothing outside will ever reply.
devices.how: Every packet is compared with policies from top to bottom: source, destination, service, action. The first match wins and the default is deny. NAT swaps private addresses for the WAN address, Virtual IPs (VIPs) forward chosen outside ports to inside servers, and static routes tell it where the internal VLANs live.
uses: WAN/LAN interfaces and the default route (Goal 2)
Outbound policies, ping policy and VIPs for FTP, SSH and HTTP
Hardening: disable ping on the WAN, change the default password
Backup the config as Goal2_Start_Backup.conf

devices.name: Backup Appliances
devices.role: Two spare firewall appliances on one rack tray
devices.what: A white rack tray holding a Netgate SG-3100 (runs pfSense) and a Fortinet FortiWiFi 60E (a FortiGate with built-in Wi-Fi). Both lift off the tray.
devices.how: Both do the same job as the main firewall: inspect and filter traffic between networks. They come from two different vendors, so students can compare pfSense with FortiOS.
uses: Standby if the main firewall is wiped or misconfigured
Hands-on comparison of two vendors' firewalls

devices.name: Auxiliary Server
devices.role: Second R440 for practice VMs and extra targets
devices.what: A second 1U R440, the same hardware as the hypervisor host.
devices.how: Same design: redundant power supplies, iDRAC remote management, two gigabit NICs and front drive carriers. Having two identical servers makes exercises possible that need a second host.
uses: Second host for practice VMs or scan targets
Hardware swap practice: drive carriers and power supplies

devices.name: Storage NAS
devices.role: Central storage for virtual machine disks
devices.what: A 4-bay network-attached storage server running DiskStation Manager (DSM). The four drives are grouped into one storage pool.
devices.how: RAID 5 spreads data and parity across the four drives, so the pool survives one drive failing. An ext4 volume holds the VM_Datastore shared folder, which is exported over NFS so a server can mount it like a local disk.
uses: Storage on its own VLAN so storage traffic is isolated (Goal 5)
VM_Datastore holds the Ubuntu-FTP disk (Goal 6)
DSM upgrade path: 6.2.4 → 7.0.1 → 7.3.2
'Mode 2' reset clears it at the end of the course
leds: green: healthy · orange blink: degraded / fault
green: drive OK · blink: activity · orange: fault

devices.name: Component Drawer
devices.role: Sliding shelf for the lab's small hardware
devices.what: A sliding 1U shelf with an open top. It stores the Raspberry Pis, cables, adapters and USB sticks.
devices.how: Telescoping rails let the shelf slide out of the rack so you can reach the contents, then lock back in. Nothing in the drawer is powered while it is stored.
uses: Inventory check at the start of every shift: tell the instructor about anything missing
Holds WEB-SRV and VULN-PI (Raspberry Pi 3)
Console cable, USB-C dongle, KVM cable and two USB sticks

devices.name: UPS Power Supply
devices.role: Battery backup that powers the rack
devices.what: A 1U, 750 VA line-interactive UPS. It conditions the wall power and keeps the rack running through a short outage.
devices.how: Wall power charges the battery. If the voltage drops or fails, an inverter switches to battery in milliseconds so equipment keeps running long enough for a safe shutdown. It also smooths surges and out-of-range voltage.
uses: Powers the whole rack through the PDU
Nightly shutdown: hold its power button, then unplug it from the wall
Protects the NAS and servers from unclean power-offs

devices.name: Rack PDU
devices.role: Power strip along the rear rail
devices.what: A vertical strip of outlets mounted at the back of the rack. It spreads one power feed to every device.
devices.how: One input feeds all outlets in parallel; each device's power cord uses one outlet. It has no battery of its own, so it depends on the UPS.
uses: Distributes power from the UPS to all devices
Keeps power cords tidy along the rail

traffic.name: Open the intranet web page
steps: The laptop asks the DHCP server on the switch for an address, then sends an HTTP request for the web page.
The core switch looks at the destination MAC address and forwards the frame only toward the web server.
WEB-SRV (Raspberry Pi) runs Apache. It reads index.html and builds the response.
The reply goes back the same way. The switch forwards it to the laptop's MAC address.
traffic.why: Static IPs, DHCP and switching working together. The firewall is not involved because the traffic never leaves the data network.

traffic.name: Reach the Internet (outbound NAT)
steps: The laptop sends a packet to an outside address. Its default gateway is the switch.
The core switch's default route points to the firewall's LAN address, so it forwards the packet there.
The firewall matches the packet against Outbound_General_Access, then NAT replaces the private source with the WAN address.
The packet leaves the WAN port toward the simulated ISP. Nothing answers because 10.0.200.1 is not a live device.
traffic.why: Default routes, firewall policy and NAT, step by step. If a hop fails, you can see which layer to check.

traffic.name: VM disk read/write over NFS
traffic.layer: Layer 4–7 · NFS on the storage VLAN
steps: A virtual machine on the hypervisor writes to its virtual disk. Proxmox turns that into NFS requests.
The requests travel to the core switch, which routes them to the Storage VLAN.
The NAS receives the request and writes it to the RAID 5 pool, spreading data and parity across the four drives.
The NAS acknowledges and the data path returns to the host. The VM never knows its disk is remote.
traffic.why: Why storage gets its own VLAN: heavy disk traffic must not slow other users.

traffic.name: Manage Proxmox from a laptop
steps: The laptop opens https://<host>:8006. Its packet is routed by the switch to the Management network.
The core switch carries the Management VLAN untagged (native) on the trunk to the host.
Proxmox answers. If the native VLAN does not match, this step fails and the page never loads.
The reply returns and the web interface appears.
traffic.why: The Native VLAN rule from Goal 3: lose the management path to the hypervisor and you lose the host.

traffic.name: Log in to the FTP server
steps: The laptop connects to the Ubuntu-FTP virtual machine and sends USER and PASS.
The switch forwards the frames. The firewall is skipped because both ends are inside.
The VM runs on the hypervisor host. Its disk is on the NAS, so reading the file list touches storage too.
The listing comes back. The login worked, and every character travelled in plain text.
traffic.why: A normal FTP session. The next demo (attack) shows what anyone watching the wire can see.

traffic.name: Local console on a server
steps: On the KVM console, choose the port the server is plugged into.
Keyboard and mouse signals go to the server; its video goes back to the screen.
No network is involved, so this works even when the network is down. That is why Proxmox is installed here first.
traffic.why: Out-of-network access: the reason a rack has a KVM.

attacks.name: Sniffing a cleartext FTP password
attacks.summary: Anyone who can see the traffic can read an FTP login.

steps.title: A user logs in
steps.text: A student starts an FTP session to Ubuntu-FTP. The password is sent as ordinary text.

steps.title: The wire is watched
steps.text: Wireshark on the analyst laptop captures frames passing the switch. FTP has no encryption, so the TCP stream contains the username and password as readable text.

steps.title: The password is read
steps.text: In the TCP stream the attacker finds the exact packet that carries PASS followed by the password.

steps.title: Impact
steps.text: With the credentials the attacker can log in to the FTP VM. Its disk is stored on the NAS, so data on the storage network is exposed too.

defend: Use SFTP or FTPS so the session is encrypted
Segment storage and management traffic onto separate VLANs
Restrict who can reach FTP with firewall policy
Monitor for unexpected captures and logins

attacks.name: Backdoor on the vulnerable Pi
attacks.summary: A web page that runs commands gives remote code execution.

steps.title: Asset discovery
steps.text: The Pi is found on the Data network by asking the switch which address it handed out by DHCP.

steps.title: Hidden page
steps.text: VULN-PI runs a web server with a backdoor page that takes a command in the URL and runs it on the server.

steps.title: Code runs
steps.text: The command runs as the web-server user. A harmless test command such as id proves the attacker controls the machine.

steps.title: Lateral movement risk
steps.text: From this foothold an attacker could probe the rest of the Data network. The switch and the firewall policy decide how far they get.

defend: Patch or remove vulnerable web software
Never leave a web shell on a server
Limit lateral movement with VLANs and firewall rules
Detect unusual requests (IDS, Greenbone scans)

attacks.name: Ping sweep and vulnerability scan
attacks.summary: Mapping a network before attacking it.

steps.title: Ping sweep
steps.text: From the target rack's Data network, Nmap sends one ICMP echo to every address in the subnet.

steps.title: Hosts answer
steps.text: Live hosts reply. The Ubuntu FTP server and the vulnerable Pi appear in the list.

steps.title: Targeted scan
steps.text: Greenbone runs a Full and Fast scan against just those IPs and reports High-severity findings.

steps.title: Firewall view
steps.text: The firewall policy blocks or allows pings between zones. Disabling ping on the WAN makes the device less visible.

defend: Turn off ping replies on exposed interfaces
Limit which networks can reach each service
Patch what the scanner finds
Log and alert on sweeps

attacks.name: Sniffing Telnet / HTTP management
attacks.summary: Admin passwords sent in cleartext can be captured.

steps.title: An admin connects
steps.text: An administrator opens the switch's web page over plain HTTP, or logs in over Telnet.

steps.title: The login is captured
steps.text: Telnet and HTTP send credentials as text. A packet capture on the path shows them.

steps.title: The attacker takes control
steps.text: With admin access the attacker can change VLANs, routes and DHCP. Every network that depends on the switch is affected.

defend: Enable SSH and HTTPS only; disable Telnet and HTTP
Use the out-of-band management port
Restrict who can reach management addresses

attacks.name: Rogue USB device (HID attack)
attacks.summary: A USB device that pretends to be a keyboard. Theory only: the lab forbids plugging these in.

steps.title: Trigger
steps.text: Someone with brief physical access plugs a device into a front USB port or the KVM. The computer trusts anything that looks like a keyboard.

steps.title: Execution
steps.text: The device types a scripted payload within seconds, as if a person were at the keyboard.

steps.title: Impact
steps.text: Whatever that account can do, the script can do. On a hypervisor that means every virtual machine and the storage it mounts.

defend: Lock the rack and use bezels
Disable unused USB ports in the BIOS
Use endpoint controls for new devices
Train staff not to plug in unknown devices

attacks.name: Probing the exposed services (VIPs)
attacks.summary: Port forwarding makes inside servers reachable from outside.

steps.title: A probe from outside
steps.text: A scan from the WAN side reaches the firewall's public address on the ports forwarded by the Virtual IPs.

steps.title: Policy decides
steps.text: The Allow_Inbound_Services policy lets FTP, SSH and HTTP through to the mapped servers. Everything else is dropped.

steps.title: Servers exposed
steps.text: The mapped FTP/SSH and web servers now answer to the outside, so they must be patched and well configured.

defend: Expose only the services you need
Keep NAT off on inbound policies so the VIP handles translation cleanly
Patch exposed servers and log connections

attacks.name: Power failure and safe shutdown
attacks.summary: The UPS buys time for an orderly shutdown.

steps.title: Wall power fails
steps.text: The UPS detects the loss and switches to battery. Its beeper sounds and the battery LED turns amber.

steps.title: Everything keeps running
steps.text: The PDU still has power, so the network, storage and servers carry on for a few minutes.

steps.title: Shut down in order
steps.text: Shut down VMs, then power off the Proxmox host, then the KVM, then the UPS. Storage and network last so nothing loses its disk.

steps.title: Battery runs out
steps.text: Without a shutdown the UPS eventually runs flat and everything powers off suddenly. A sudden power-off can corrupt a RAID volume or a VM disk.

defend: Size the UPS for the load and runtime
Configure automatic shutdown on the NAS and servers
Test the battery regularly

attacks.name: Native VLAN mismatch
attacks.summary: One setting on a trunk cuts off the hypervisor.

steps.title: Misconfiguration
steps.text: The trunk toward the hypervisor is set without the Management VLAN as the native (untagged) VLAN.

steps.title: Host unreachable
steps.text: The host sends untagged management frames, but the switch expects tagged ones. They land in the wrong VLAN or are dropped.

steps.title: Knock-on effects
steps.text: The Proxmox web page times out. VMs and NFS storage lose their path as well.

steps.title: Fix it bottom-up
steps.text: Check Layer 1 link lights first, then Layer 2 VLAN and trunk settings, then Layer 3 addresses, then Layer 4–7 policy.

defend: Use the OSI bottom-up method
Change one thing at a time
Back up the config before changing trunks

Check VLAN assignments, trunk status and the MAC address table.
Check IP and mask, the default gateway and routing tables.
Check firewall policies, service status and ports.
